annotations.text: World models that predict environment dynamics can serve as pre-execution verifiers for agents facing irreversible actions. However, sequential verify-and-retry— where rejected actions trigger agent re-planning—can paradoxically reduce task success as verification budget increases. We identify trajectory drift as the root cause: when verification rejects a checkout (often a false negative), the agent rebrowses and frequently selects a worse product than originally found. We propose chunked budget allocation: instead of spreading verification budget across many sequential cycles, spend it in fewer cycles with more parallel rollouts per cycle. On WebShop, chunked verification (M = 1 cycle) achieves 21.50% task success versus 0.86% for sequential verify-and-retry (M = 10 cycles)—a 25× improvement at the same budget. Surprisingly, consensus aggregation across parallel rollouts provides no benefit over single-rollout acceptance, as the world model’s poor calibration (predicting failure for 98.4% of cycles) causes consensus to degenerate. Our results demonstrate that budget allocation structure matters more than aggregation sophistication when world models are poorly calibrated.
annotations.comment:
Page 1 - Abstract

Problem (claim/evidence alignment): The abstract mixes three distinct ideas—(i) *budget allocation across sequential cycles* (M vs. K), (ii) *aggregation rule* (consensus vs. single rollout), and (iii) a very large headline gain (21.50% vs 0.86%)—but it is not explicit that the 21.50% result corresponds to the **no-aggregation** chunked variant (Condition C) rather than the consensus method (Condition B). This can mislead readers about what the proposed method actually is. It also implicitly suggests broad “verification budget increases hurt” generality, while the evidence in this paper is limited to one environment/model pair.

Why it matters: For a short paper, the abstract is the main contract with the reader. If the method/result mapping is ambiguous, reviewers may interpret the contribution as “we propose consensus chunking” but the strongest result comes from a different decision rule. Also, without a *no-verification* baseline (B=0), the magnitude of improvement is hard to interpret: chunking might mainly behave like “stop rejecting repeatedly” rather than adding useful verification.

Actionable fix (content + defensible scope):
- Explicitly name which chunked variant achieves 21.50% (e.g., “M=1 with single-rollout acceptance”).
- Add one short phrase bounding scope: “in this WebShop setting with a poorly calibrated verifier”.
- If space allows, report (or promise in the paper) a no-verification baseline to contextualize whether chunking beats simply not verifying.

Mentor Revised Version:
World-model verifiers are often used to screen irreversible actions (e.g., checkout) in web agents. We show that a standard sequential verify-and-retry loop can reduce WebShop task success as more verification cycles are allowed, because rejected checkouts trigger re-browsing that drifts the trajectory away from previously good candidates. We study budget allocation under a fixed number of world-model calls $B$ by distributing calls across $M$ verification cycles with $K=B/M$ parallel rollouts per cycle; smaller $M$ reduces verification-induced re-planning. On WebShop (Gemini-2.5-Flash actor; fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B verifier) allocating the full budget to a single cycle ($M=1$, $K=10$) achieves 21.50% success with single-rollout acceptance, versus 0.86% for the sequential baseline ($M\approx10$, $K=1$) at the same $B=10$. In this setting, consensus aggregation does not help because the verifier is extremely under-confident (98.4% of cycles yield $\hat p=0$), suggesting allocation structure can dominate aggregation when verifiers are poorly calibrated.

References:
[4] Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents 2506.12928

[9] ARTIS: Agentic Risk-Aware Test-Time Scaling via Iterative Simulation 2602.01709
annotations.summary: Abstract is clear on the phenomenon, but it conflates which “chunked” variant achieves 21.5% and over-extends claims without a no-verification baseline or scoped generalization.

annotations.text: World models that predict environment dynamics have emerged as a powerful tool for agent decision-making (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Schrittwieser et al., 2019). For agents operating in environments with irreversible actions—such as submitting purchases, sending emails, or deleting files—world models can serve as pre-execution verifiers: before committing to a high-stakes action, the agent queries the world model to predict whether the action will succeed. Recent work has demonstrated this approach for web agents, using LLM-based world models to verify checkout actions before execution (Li et al., 2025; Gu et al., 2025).
annotations.comment:
Page 1 - Introduction (Paragraph 1: motivation + prior work)

Problem: This paragraph sets up “world models as pre-execution verifiers” and cites prior web-agent world-model work, but it blurs two different uses of world models: (i) model-based planning/search (simulate transitions to choose actions) and (ii) *verification* of a proposed irreversible action. Because the rest of the paper is about verification budget allocation, readers need a sharper statement of the *specific gap*: not “world models exist,” but “world-model verification + retry can regress with more budget in irreversible settings.” Also, “world model” is used broadly; later you use a fine-tuned Qwen model predicting next observation + success indicator, which is a particular operational definition.

Why it matters: Novelty and contribution are easiest to reject when the problem statement does not crisply distinguish the paper’s setting from adjacent model-based planning literature (e.g., using world models for deliberation over action outcomes). This is especially important because prior work explicitly discusses irreversible actions on the web and uses world-model simulation for decision-making.

Actionable fix:
- Add a one-sentence operational definition: in this paper, the verifier predicts a binary task-success outcome for a candidate irreversible action given the current trajectory history.
- Add a one-sentence gap statement that foreshadows non-monotonic regressions under sequential verify-and-retry.
- Add a short clause contrasting with model-based planning (you are not proposing search/planning; you are analyzing budget allocation for a verifier).

Mentor Revised Version:
World models can help web agents avoid costly irreversible mistakes by *predicting the outcome of a proposed action before execution*. In this paper, we focus on a verifier-style world model that, given the current trajectory history, predicts whether a candidate irreversible action (here: checkout) will satisfy the user intent. This differs from model-based planning methods that use simulated rollouts to *choose* actions via search: our setting assumes the agent already proposes a checkout and the world model is queried only to accept or block it. A key open question is how to use a fixed verification budget effectively in such irreversible environments, since sequential “verify-and-retry” loops can change the agent’s future trajectory after each rejection.

References:
[1] Is Your LLM Secretly a World Model of the Internet? Model-Based Planning for Web Agents 2411.06559

[2] Web Agents with World Models: Learning and Leveraging Environment Dynamics in Web Navigation 2410.13232
annotations.summary: Intro P1 motivates world-model verification well, but needs sharper gap framing (verification vs planning), clearer definition of “world model” in this paper, and tighter related-work positioning.

annotations.text: However, a counterintuitive failure mode has been observed: increasing the verification budget (the number of world-model queries allowed) can reduce task success rates (Li et al., 2025). This nonmonotonic behavior occurs because sequential verify-and-retry creates a problematic feedback loop. When verification rejects a checkout (potentially a false negative), the agent re-browses to find another product. During re-browsing, the agent often selects a worse product than the one originally found—a phenomenon we call trajectory drift. More verification cycles mean more opportunities for trajectory drift.
annotations.comment:
Page 1 - Introduction (Paragraph 2: non-monotonicity + trajectory drift)

Problem: This paragraph asserts a strong causal story: more verification budget → more sequential cycles → more false-negative rejections → re-browsing → worse product → lower success (“trajectory drift”). The paper later provides a failure-pattern table, but the current paragraph reads like a complete explanation without acknowledging alternative mechanisms (e.g., verifier thresholding effects, acting-agent exploration temperature, or budget exhaustion rule “auto-pass after M cycles” changing behavior). Also, “often a false negative” is plausible but not quantified here; readers need an explicit statement of what evidence will be shown.

Why it matters: The paper’s value hinges on identifying the *right* mechanism. If trajectory drift is only one contributor, or if the observed effect is partially an artifact of decision thresholds or policy changes after budget exhaustion, reviewers will question the generality of the recommendation “set M=1.”

Actionable fix:
- In this paragraph, downgrade causal language to “suggests/is consistent with” and preview the specific evidence you will provide (e.g., the fraction of failures attributable to re-browsing and an estimate of verifier false negative rate conditioned on ground-truth success).
- Add one sentence naming at least one alternative hypothesis you will rule out later (e.g., threshold/consensus interaction, acting-agent stochasticity).

Mentor Revised Version:
Prior work reports a counterintuitive failure mode: allowing more verifier queries can reduce end-to-end task success in WebShop-style settings. We hypothesize that this regression is largely driven by *trajectory drift*: when a verifier blocks an initially good checkout (potentially due to false negatives), the agent re-enters browsing and may settle on an inferior product, so additional verify-and-retry cycles create more opportunities to drift away from an earlier good candidate. In Section 4, we test this hypothesis by (i) comparing different allocations of the same verification budget across sequential cycles, and (ii) categorizing failures to measure how often re-browsing after a rejection precedes the eventual mistake. We also examine alternative explanations such as threshold/aggregation effects and decoding stochasticity.

References:
[4] Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents 2506.12928

[5] DynScaling: Efficient Verifier-free Inference Scaling via Dynamic and Integrated Sampling 2506.16043
annotations.summary: Intro P2 claims non-monotonicity due to trajectory drift; it needs clearer causal evidence, alternative explanations, and a more defensible wording that matches the provided failure analysis.

annotations.text: The key insight is that the problem lies not in verification accuracy, but in the sequential structure of verify-and-retry. Each rejection triggers re-browsing, compounding errors across cycles. This suggests a simple solution: instead of spreading the verification budget across many sequential cycles, spend it in fewer cycles with more parallel rollouts per cycle.
annotations.comment:
Page 1 - Introduction (Paragraph 3: “key insight”)

Problem: The paragraph states “the problem lies not in verification accuracy, but in the sequential structure,” which is too absolute given later evidence that the verifier is *poorly calibrated* and has a high false-negative tendency. A more defensible claim is conditional: even with imperfect verifiers, sequential rejection-induced re-planning can dominate outcomes; structural choices interact with verifier error rates.

Why it matters: Reviewers will push back on causal overreach (“not accuracy”) because the paper itself argues consensus fails due to calibration (an accuracy/uncertainty quality issue). The scientific contribution is stronger if you frame an interaction: structure × calibration × re-planning dynamics.

Actionable fix:
- Rephrase to: “the regression is driven by the interaction between verifier errors and the sequential verify-and-retry structure.”
- Add one sentence connecting to test-time compute allocation in agents: you are studying *how to spend a fixed budget* (parallel vs sequential) for safety-critical/irreversible steps, which relates to broader test-time scaling strategies.

Mentor Revised Version:
A key observation is that non-monotonic regressions can arise from an *interaction* between verifier errors (e.g., under-confident or miscalibrated predictions) and the sequential verify-and-retry structure: each rejection triggers re-browsing, so even occasional false negatives can push the agent onto worse trajectories over time. This motivates viewing verification as a test-time compute allocation problem in an agentic setting: under a fixed world-model query budget, should we spend compute sequentially across many retries, or concentrate it into fewer decision points with more parallel rollouts?

References:
[4] Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents 2506.12928

[5] Uncertainty-Aware Budget Allocation for Adaptive Test-Time Reasoning 2605.26849
annotations.summary: Intro P3’s ‘key insight’ over-commits to structure over accuracy; strengthen by stating required conditions and by connecting to existing test-time scaling/budget-allocation literature.

annotations.text: We propose chunked budget allocation: given a fixed verification budget B, allocate it across M cycles with K = B/M parallel world-model rollouts per cycle. By setting M = 1, we spend the entire budget in one parallel chunk, eliminating the sequential cycles that trigger trajectory drift. Our contributions are:
annotations.comment:
Page 1 - Introduction (Paragraph 4: method definition + contributions lead-in)

Problem: The definition “allocate budget B across M cycles with K=B/M parallel rollouts per cycle” is clear, but the paragraph omits key operational details needed to interpret the rest of the paper:
- What exactly is a “cycle” (is it “each time the agent proposes checkout”)?
- When a checkout is blocked, does the agent continue with the same policy and same context window? Is there any memory of the previously found good product?
- How is the decision made in the chunked case (consensus threshold vs first rollout), and how is $\tau$ chosen?

These omissions make the upcoming comparisons feel like black-box configurations rather than a well-defined algorithmic family.

Why it matters: The core scientific claim is that *allocation structure* causes the performance change. To make this causal story credible and reproducible, the reader needs a precise algorithm definition, especially because rejection changes the agent’s subsequent observation distribution.

Actionable fix:
- Add a short formal definition: “A cycle is triggered whenever the actor proposes checkout; the verifier returns accept/block; if block, the actor continues from the current environment state for up to 50 steps.”
- Add explicit decision rules and hyperparameters ($\tau$ for consensus, auto-pass rule when budget exhausted) in this paragraph or immediately after.
- Tighten the contribution list to match what is actually tested (and avoid overclaiming that the guidance is universal).

Mentor Revised Version:
We study a family of verifier policies under a fixed budget of $B$ world-model calls per episode. Each time the actor proposes an irreversible action (checkout), we run one *verification cycle*: we query the world model $K$ times from the current trajectory state, aggregate these rollouts into an accept/block decision (e.g., by thresholding $\hat p$ or using a single rollout), and if blocked, the actor continues browsing in the real environment until the next checkout proposal. We allocate the same total budget across $M$ cycles with $K=B/M$ rollouts per cycle. Our hypothesis is that smaller $M$ reduces rejection-induced re-planning and thus mitigates trajectory drift.

References:
[1] Is Your LLM Secretly a World Model of the Internet? Model-Based Planning for Web Agents 2411.06559

[9] ARTIS: Agentic Risk-Aware Test-Time Scaling via Iterative Simulation 2602.01709
annotations.summary: Intro P4 defines chunked allocation (M,K) but lacks decision policy details (thresholding, what happens on rejection, what if multiple checkout attempts) and a stronger contributions preview tied to later evidence.

annotations.text: Web Agents. The development of autonomous web agents has been driven by increasingly realistic benchmarks. WebShop (Yao et al., 2022) introduced a simulated e-commerce environment where agents must navigate product search and purchase workflows. WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023) extended this to self-hosted websites with more complex, multi-step tasks. Mind2Web (Deng et al., 2023) provided a large-scale dataset of real-world web interactions across diverse domains, while WebVoyager (He et al., 2024) demonstrated end-to-end web navigation using multimodal models. We use WebShop as our testbed due to its well-defined irreversible action (checkout) and established evaluation protocol.
annotations.comment:
Page 2 - Related Work (Web Agents paragraph)

Problem: The paragraph enumerates benchmarks (WebShop/WebArena/Mind2Web/WebVoyager) but does not articulate the *comparison axis* that matters for this paper (irreversible actions + evaluation protocol + whether retries are allowed). As written, it feels like a generic benchmark survey rather than positioning for a verification-budget-allocation study.

Why it matters: Your paper’s thesis is about verification for irreversible actions; the related work should teach the reader why WebShop is the right “minimal” environment for isolating this phenomenon, and what the missing evidence is for broader generality (e.g., real websites, multimodal, longer horizons).

Actionable fix:
- Add 1–2 sentences that define the axis: “irreversible commit action with episode termination” and “rule-based success metric”.
- Briefly justify why WebShop, despite being simulated, is appropriate for isolating verify-and-retry regressions.

Mentor Revised Version:
Web-agent benchmarks differ not only in UI realism but also in whether they contain *irreversible commit actions* that terminate an episode and make backtracking infeasible. WebShop provides a controlled setting with an explicit irreversible checkout step and a standardized success metric, which makes it suitable for isolating how verifier decisions interact with sequential retries. In contrast, benchmarks such as WebArena, Mind2Web, and WebVoyager increase website realism and modality, but also introduce additional confounders (dynamic pages, multimodal grounding, longer horizons) that we leave to future generalization tests.

References:
[8] AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories 2504.08942
annotations.summary: Related Work ‘Web Agents’ paragraph is informative but reads like a list; strengthen by stating the comparison axis and how WebShop’s irreversible checkout property connects to your verification setting.

annotations.text: World Models for Agents. World models that predict environment dynamics have shown promise for agent planning. Classical approaches (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018; Schrittwieser et al., 2019) learn latent dynamics models for game environments. Recent work has explored LLMs as implicit world models for web agents: WebDreamer (Gu et al., 2025) uses LLMs to simulate web page transitions for model-based planning, Word2World (Li et al., 2025) investigates whether LLMs can serve as text-based world simulators, and DynaWeb (Ding et al., 2026) applies model-based reinforcement learning to web navigation. Chae et al. (2024) train world models to predict HTML state transitions. Our work is complementary: rather than improving world model accuracy, we study how to allocate a fixed verification budget effectively.
annotations.comment:
Page 2 - Related Work (World Models for Agents paragraph)

Problem: This paragraph correctly cites prior LLM world-model work for web agents, but the positioning is still somewhat generic (“complementary”). Given retrieval evidence, prior work already emphasizes irreversible actions and using world models to simulate outcomes before committing (model-based planning). The manuscript’s novelty is *not* “world models for web agents,” but “how to allocate a fixed verification/query budget across sequential vs parallel verification cycles to avoid regression.” That core differentiation is not made explicit.

Why it matters: Without an explicit head-to-head overlap statement, novelty risk is high: a reviewer can argue that your setting is a special case of prior “simulate before commit” approaches (e.g., pre-execution deliberation), and that the paper is mainly an ablation of K vs M with a particular verifier.

Actionable fix:
- Add a short paragraph at the end of this subsection that states: (i) what prior work optimizes (world-model fidelity/planning/search), (ii) what you hold fixed (verifier model), and (iii) what you study (budget allocation + sequential feedback effects).
- Cite the closest overlaps explicitly and state the new failure mode + design rule.

Mentor Revised Version:
Prior work leverages LLM-based world models to improve web agents primarily by increasing world-model fidelity or using simulated rollouts for planning and policy selection. In contrast, we hold the verifier model fixed and study a different question: under a fixed per-episode query budget, how should verification compute be allocated across sequential verify-and-retry cycles versus parallel rollouts at a single decision point? We show that, for irreversible commit actions, sequential rejection-induced re-planning can cause trajectory drift that overwhelms the benefits of additional verification.

References:
[1] Is Your LLM Secretly a World Model of the Internet? Model-Based Planning for Web Agents 2411.06559

[2] Web Agents with World Models: Learning and Leveraging Environment Dynamics in Web Navigation 2410.13232

[3] From Word to World: Can Large Language Models be Implicit Text-based World Models? 2512.18832
annotations.summary: World-model related work should more explicitly separate planning vs verification and clarify overlap with WebDreamer/WMA; add a sharper ‘what is new here’ paragraph tied to budget-allocation structure.

annotations.text: Test-Time Scaling. Scaling compute at test time has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving LLM performance. Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) samples multiple reasoning paths and aggregates via majority voting. Recent work extends this to agentic settings: Lee et al. (2026) study test-time scaling for web agents, and Zhu et al. (2025) investigate compute allocation strategies for LLM agents. Our findings reveal a surprising limitation: for verification of irreversible actions, the allocation structure (chunked vs. sequential) matters more than the aggregation rule (consensus vs. first-rollout).
annotations.comment:
Page 2 - Related Work (Test-Time Scaling paragraph)

Problem: The paragraph claims “allocation structure matters more than aggregation rule,” but it does not connect to existing test-time scaling findings that (a) sequential reflection can hurt if applied indiscriminately, and (b) compute allocation should be adaptive to uncertainty. Also, your “consensus fails” explanation is really about confidence estimation/calibration collapse (mass at $\hat p=0$), which has parallels in LLM confidence estimation and LLM-as-a-judge calibration literature.

Why it matters: This is where you can make the paper feel like more than a one-off WebShop ablation. By grounding your claim in known test-time scaling/control phenomena, you can position chunking as an *agentic compute allocation* principle for irreversible commits.

Actionable fix:
- Add one sentence acknowledging that prior test-time scaling often finds positive effects from parallel sampling, but sequential strategies can degrade long-horizon performance when they repeatedly perturb the trajectory.
- Add one sentence situating your consensus failure as a calibration issue and referencing relevant calibration work.

Mentor Revised Version:
Test-time scaling for LLM agents spans both parallel sampling and sequential revision/reflection. While more compute often helps, sequential interventions can also degrade long-horizon trajectories when they repeatedly alter the agent’s state distribution after each rejection or revision. Our results highlight a complementary axis for agentic settings with irreversible actions: under a fixed query budget, concentrating verification compute into fewer decision points can reduce harmful sequential feedback loops. We further observe that naive consensus can fail when verifier confidence is severely miscalibrated, aligning with broader findings on confidence estimation and calibration for LLM-based judges.

References:
[4] Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents 2506.12928

[6] When Can We Trust LLM Graders? Calibrating Confidence for Automated Assessment 2603.29559

[7] A Survey of Confidence Estimation and Calibration in Large Language Models 2311.08298
annotations.summary: Test-time scaling paragraph could be stronger by connecting to sequential-vs-parallel compute tradeoffs and by clarifying that your ‘consensus fails’ result is partly a calibration/uncertainty-estimation issue known in prior work.

annotations.text: Error Recovery in Agents. Agents inevitably make mistakes, motivating error recovery mechanisms. Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) enables agents to learn from verbal feedback on failed attempts. WebRollback (Zhang et al., 2025) introduces explicit rollback mechanisms for web agents to recover from errors. However, these approaches assume that retry improves outcomes. We show that for irreversible actions, sequential retry can cause trajectory drift, where rejected checkouts trigger re-browsing that leads to worse product selections.
annotations.comment:
Page 2 - Related Work (Error Recovery in Agents paragraph)

Problem: The paragraph states “these approaches assume retry improves outcomes,” which is not always accurate: rollback/backtracking methods often explicitly manage recovery. The real distinction for your work is narrower: even with recovery mechanisms, repeated retry that changes the browsing trajectory can degrade final selection under irreversible commits, especially when the verifier has a high false-negative rate.

Why it matters: Overstating assumptions about prior work can backfire in review. A precise contrast improves credibility and helps define the boundary conditions of “trajectory drift.”

Actionable fix:
- Replace “assume retry improves outcomes” with a more bounded statement: “typically aim to make retries effective via reflection/rollback, but do not study the budget-allocation-induced regression mechanism in verifier-gated irreversible commits.”

Mentor Revised Version:
Prior error-recovery mechanisms (e.g., reflection, rollback/backtracking) aim to make retries more effective by using feedback or state restoration. Our focus is different: in verifier-gated irreversible commits, repeated *re-planning after a blocked commit* can change what the agent subsequently browses and selects, so additional retry opportunities can systematically increase the chance of drifting away from an initially good candidate when the verifier is under-confident.

References:
[2] Web Agents with World Models: Learning and Leveraging Environment Dynamics in Web Navigation 2410.13232
annotations.summary: Error-recovery paragraph asserts retries assume improvement; refine by contrasting with rollback/backtracking work and stating your setting’s ‘irreversible commit + verifier false negatives’ mechanism more precisely.

annotations.text: We study world-model verification for irreversible actions in the WebShop environment (Yao et al., 2022), a text-based e-commerce benchmark where an agent must navigate product search and complete purchases. The agent receives text observations describing search results and product pages, and takes actions such as searching, clicking products, and checking out. Checkout is an irreversible action: once executed, the episode terminates regardless of whether the purchase matches the user’s intent.
annotations.comment:
Page 2 - Method (3.1 Problem Setup)

Problem: The environment and irreversibility are described well, but key protocol details needed to reproduce and interpret the results are missing here:
- When does the agent decide to propose “checkout” (is it a learned/prompted action each step, or only from a product page)?
- Is WebShop deterministic given an action sequence (important for reasoning about retries and drift)?
- How exactly is “purchase matches user intent” computed (rule-based string match? WebShop’s official evaluator details)?
- What is the baseline when no verification is used (B=0), and is it comparable to your conditions?

Why it matters: Your central claim is about *decision dynamics* under rejection; small protocol differences (termination rules, allowed actions, evaluator) can change whether sequential retries help or hurt. Missing setup details also makes the reported absolute success rates hard to contextualize.

Actionable fix:
- Add 3–5 sentences here defining: action space constraints around checkout; deterministic vs stochastic environment aspects; the exact success evaluation; and a “no verification” baseline used for sanity.

Mentor Revised Version:
We study verifier-gated checkout in WebShop, where the agent may execute a checkout action at any step after navigating to a specific product page. Checkout is irreversible: once executed, the episode terminates and success is scored by the WebShop official evaluator based on whether the purchased item satisfies the task constraints (e.g., attributes and price). Throughout this paper we report success rate under a fixed maximum of 50 interaction steps and compare against a no-verification baseline ($B=0$) to isolate whether verification is beneficial beyond simply reducing retries.

References:
[8] AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories 2504.08942
annotations.summary: Problem setup is clear, but reproducibility requires more protocol specifics (when checkout is proposed, environment determinism, success labeling); add these and a no-verification baseline definition here.

annotations.text: Our setup uses Gemini-2.5-Flash as the acting agent and a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B model as the world model (Li et al., 2025). Given the current trajectory history h and a candidate action $^ { a , }$ the world model predicts the next observation $s ^ { \prime }$ and a binary success indicator $R ^ { \prime } \in \{ 0 , 1 \}$ . For checkout verification, R′ indicates whether the purchase would satisfy the user’s intent.
annotations.comment:
Page 3 - Method (end of 3.1 Problem Setup)

Problem: The paragraph specifies the acting agent (Gemini-2.5-Flash) and verifier (fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B) but omits details necessary to reproduce or even interpret the reported failure modes:
- Acting agent prompt template and whether it is allowed to see verifier outputs.
- Context window/history truncation policy for $h$ (important for “trajectory drift”).
- World model fine-tuning data source/size/objective: is it trained on WebShop trajectories? Does it predict both $s'$ and $R'$ jointly? How is $R'$ supervised?
- Sampling parameters are given later, but not whether $R'$ is sampled or deterministic.
Also, there is a notation/extraction issue: “candidate action $^{a,}$” is unclear and looks like a formatting bug.

Why it matters: The core claim depends on false negatives and calibration; these are properties of the verifier model and its training. Without training/evaluation details, readers cannot know whether the phenomenon is general or an artifact of a specific fine-tuning recipe.

Actionable fix:
- Add a short “Implementation details” paragraph (or appendix) describing the actor prompt, max context length and truncation, and verifier fine-tuning procedure.
- Fix the action notation and consistently denote action as $a$.

Mentor Revised Version:
Our setup uses Gemini-2.5-Flash as the acting policy and a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B model as the world-model verifier. Given the trajectory history $h$ and a candidate checkout action $a$, the verifier produces a predicted next observation $s'$ and a binary success indicator $R'\in\{0,1\}$ indicating whether executing checkout would satisfy the user intent. For reproducibility, we provide (i) the full actor prompt and whether verifier feedback is included in the actor context, (ii) the history truncation policy used to construct $h$, and (iii) the verifier fine-tuning dataset and objective used to supervise $R'$.

References:
[3] From Word to World: Can Large Language Models be Implicit Text-based World Models? 2512.18832
annotations.summary: Method setup defines actor/verifier models but is missing critical reproducibility details (prompting, context window, verifier training data). Also fix notation glitch around candidate action a.

annotations.text:
Given a verification budget B (maximum world-model calls per episode), we consider how to allocate this budget across M verification cycles, with $K = B / \dot { M }$ parallel rollouts per cycle. When the agent proposes checkout, we generate K independent stochastic world-model predictions from the current state and compute the consensus estimate:
$$
\hat {p} = \frac {1}{K} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {K} \mathbb {1} [ R _ {k} ^ {\prime} = 1 ] \tag {1}
$$
The checkout proceeds if $\hat { p } \geq \tau$ (threshold), otherwise it is blocked and the agent continues browsing. After M cycles, any subsequent checkout attempt automatically passes (budget exhausted).
annotations.comment:
Page 3 - Method (3.2 Verification Framework)

Problem: The framework defines $\hat p$ and a threshold rule, but several details are underspecified and can materially change outcomes:
1) “After M cycles, any subsequent checkout attempt automatically passes” is a strong policy choice that may inflate success (or induce failures) compared to alternatives (e.g., stop the episode, or keep blocking). It also couples performance to when the agent first proposes checkout.
2) It is unclear whether a “cycle” is consumed only when the agent proposes checkout, and whether multiple checkout proposals can occur (likely yes).
3) How is $\tau$ selected? In later experiments $\tau$ varies (0.1 vs 0.5), and the observed non-monotonicity partially depends on this interaction. Without a principled selection rule (calibration set, fixed across M, etc.), the comparison may be unfair.

Why it matters: Your main claims are about budget allocation structure. If auto-pass and $\tau$ choices change, the claimed mechanism could partially be a policy artifact rather than an inherent structural effect. This is a validity/reproducibility risk.

Actionable fix:
- Add an explicit “Algorithm 1” pseudocode (or boxed procedure) defining: when cycles are consumed, what happens on reject, what happens on budget exhausted, and which decision rule is used in each condition.
- Add an acceptance-criteria section: define $\tau$ selection protocol (e.g., fixed global value chosen on a dev set) and keep it constant across compared methods unless explicitly studied.

Mentor Revised Version:
We define a verification cycle as the event when the actor proposes checkout. In cycle $m\le M$, we query the world model $K=B/M$ times from the current trajectory state, compute $\hat p=(1/K)\sum_k \mathbb{1}[R_k'=1]$, and execute checkout iff $\hat p\ge \tau$; otherwise checkout is blocked and the actor continues browsing. If the actor proposes checkout after $M$ consumed cycles, we either (a) execute checkout unconditionally (auto-pass; used in this study) or (b) terminate/abstain; we report both variants in ablations. Unless otherwise stated, $\tau$ is selected once on a held-out validation set and fixed across all $M$.

References:
[6] When Can We Trust LLM Graders? Calibrating Confidence for Automated Assessment 2603.29559

[7] A Survey of Confidence Estimation and Calibration in Large Language Models 2311.08298
annotations.summary: Verification framework leaves key decision-policy edge cases unclear (budget exhaustion auto-pass; multiple checkout attempts; threshold τ selection). This ambiguity can change results and needs a precise algorithm box.

annotations.text:
We compare three verification strategies at the same budget $B = 1 0 !$
Condition A (Sequential Verify-and-Retry). The standard approach from prior work (Li et al., 2025): each checkout proposal triggers a single world-model query $( K = 1 )$ . If $R ^ { \prime } = 1$ , checkout proceeds; if $R ^ { \prime } = 0$ , checkout is blocked and the agent continues. This allows up to M ≈ 10 verification cycles.
Condition B (Chunked Consensus). Our proposed approach: spend the entire budget in $M = 1$ cycle with $K = 1 0$ parallel rollouts. Checkout proceeds if $\hat { p } \geq \tau$ (we use $\tau = 0 . 1 )$ . This eliminates sequential verification cycles that could trigger trajectory drift.
Condition C (Chunked No-Aggregation). A control condition with the same structure as B (M = 1, K = 10) but without consensus aggregation: only the first rollout’s R′ determines the decision. This isolates whether gains come from reducing cycles (shared by B and C) or from consensus aggregation (only in B).
annotations.comment:
Page 3 - Method (3.3 Experimental Conditions)

Problem: The three conditions are meant to isolate structure vs aggregation, but the current definition creates comparability/interpretation issues:
- Condition B uses consensus with $\tau=0.1$, while later mechanism analysis discusses $\tau=0.5$ interactions and temperature ablation uses $M=2,K=5,\tau=0.5$. This makes it hard to know whether B underperforms C because of aggregation per se, or because the chosen threshold is suboptimal under miscalibration.
- Condition C “first-rollout acceptance” is not just “no aggregation”; it changes the effective decision rule in a way that can systematically increase pass probability when the model is under-confident (because consensus averages many zeros). This is *the* point of your finding, but it should be framed as: “consensus is brittle under extreme under-confidence; single-sample decision can be less brittle.”

Why it matters: The strongest causal claims (“consensus provides no benefit”) require a fair comparison across thresholds/decision rules. Otherwise reviewers can argue the conclusion is an artifact of one chosen $\tau$.

Actionable fix:
- Add a controlled sweep: for fixed $M=1,K=10$, evaluate multiple $\tau$ values for consensus (including very low thresholds) and compare to alternative aggregators (max, softmax, any-positive) that are natural under under-confidence.
- Clarify the hypothesis test: (H1) structure effect (M) vs (H2) aggregation/decision-rule effect given calibration.

Mentor Revised Version:
We compare (A) sequential verify-and-retry ($M\approx B, K=1$), (B) chunked parallel verification with consensus thresholding, and (C) chunked parallel verification with a single-sample decision. To separate allocation effects from decision-rule effects, we additionally sweep the consensus threshold $\tau$ for (B) under the same $M=1,K=10$ setting and report which $\tau$ maximizes performance. We interpret any residual gap between (B) and (C) as evidence that, under severe under-confidence, majority-style aggregation can be brittle.

References:
[6] When Can We Trust LLM Graders? Calibrating Confidence for Automated Assessment 2603.29559
annotations.summary: Experimental conditions are not strictly comparable: B uses consensus τ=0.1 while later analysis assumes τ=0.5; and Condition C ‘first-rollout’ is biased vs consensus. Need a fair decision-rule sweep and clearer hypothesis test.

annotations.text:
Table 1 presents our main findings. Chunked verification dramatically outperforms sequential verify-and-retry at the same budget $B ~ = ~ 1 0$ . Condition C (chunked, no aggregation) achieves 21.50% success rate, a 25× improvement over Condition A (sequential) at 0.86%. The paired bootstrap confidence interval for C−A is [+17.50, +24.00] percentage points, confirming the improvement is statistically significant.
Surprisingly, consensus aggregation (Condition B) does not improve over the simpler first-rollout pass-through (Condition C). Condition C outperforms B by $6 . 6 7$ percentage points, suggesting that the benefit comes from reducing sequential cycles rather than from aggregation. We investigate this mechanism in the following sections.
annotations.comment:
Page 4 - Experiments (4.2 Main Results)

Verification checks (F1/F2): The 25× figure is arithmetically consistent with 21.50% / 0.86% ≈ 25.0, and the reported CI suggests a large effect. However, the causal interpretation “benefit comes from reducing sequential cycles” is not fully justified by the presented conditions because Condition C differs from Condition B not only in structure but also in *decision rule* (single-rollout vs consensus) and likely effective pass probability under an under-confident verifier.

Why it matters: The paper’s main claim could be reframed as either:
(A) “allocate budget to fewer cycles” (structure effect), or
(B) “avoid averaging under-confident rollouts; use a more permissive acceptance rule” (decision-rule/calibration effect).
Without cleanly separating A vs B, reviewers may argue the method is “just accept more checkouts earlier,” which weakens the scientific contribution.

Actionable fix:
- Add a no-verification baseline ($B=0$) and report A/B/C relative to it.
- Add a matched-threshold comparison: fix $\tau$ across B and the M-sweep, or explicitly tune $\tau$ on a dev set and report tuned values.
- Add an analysis table: for each condition, report (i) #checkout proposals, (ii) pass rate, (iii) false-negative rate estimated on cycles with successful ground-truth checkout, (iv) average steps to checkout.

Mentor Revised Version:
Table 1 shows a large improvement from chunked verification, but to attribute the gain to *cycle reduction* rather than the decision rule, we also report (i) a no-verification baseline ($B=0$), (ii) consensus results under a tuned or fixed $\tau$ across conditions, and (iii) per-condition pass statistics (checkout proposal count, block rate, and estimated false-negative rate). This decomposition clarifies whether performance is driven primarily by fewer sequential re-planning events (smaller $M$) or by a more permissive acceptance rule under severe under-confidence.

References:
[6] When Can We Trust LLM Graders? Calibrating Confidence for Automated Assessment 2603.29559
annotations.summary: Main-results claims are numerically consistent, but interpretation is underspecified: need a B=0 baseline, matched τ across conditions, and a decomposition of ‘structure vs decision rule’ before attributing gains to cycle reduction alone.

annotations.text:
To isolate the effect of verification cycle count, we vary $M \in \{ 1 , 2 , 5 , 1 0 \}$ while keeping the total budget $B = 1 0$ fixed (so $K = B / M )$ . Figure 2 shows the results. The pattern is striking: $M = 1$ (all budget in one parallel chunk) achieves 20.0% success, while $M = 1 0$ (sequential, $\bar { K } = 1$ per cycle) achieves only $0 . 8 3 \% - { \tt a } 2 4 \times$ difference.
The intermediate values show a non-monotonic pattern: $M = 2 ( 8 . 5 \% )$ performs worse than $M = 5$ (14.0%). This is explained by the interaction between K and the consensus threshold τ : with $K = 5$ rollouts and $\tau = 0 . 5 ,$ , passing requires at least 3 positive predictions, which is difficult given the world model’s high false-negative rate. With $K = 2$ and $\tau = 0 . 5 ,$ , passing requires both rollouts to predict success, which is even harder. The key insight is that the extremes $( \mathbf { \dot { M } } = 1 \mathrm { v s } M = 1 0 )$ show the clearest pattern: fewer sequential cycles lead to dramatically better outcomes.
annotations.comment:
Page 4 - Experiments (4.3 Mechanism Analysis: Cycle Reduction)

Problem: The M-sweep mixes three moving parts: $M$ changes (sequential depth), $K=B/M$ changes (parallel width), and the effective strictness of consensus changes via $\tau$ and integer rounding (“needs 3 positives out of 5”, etc.). The paragraph explains the intermediate non-monotonicity by threshold interaction, which is plausible, but it also means the sweep is not a clean test of “sequential cycles harm.” Additionally, the figure description does not report CIs for each M value in the text/table.

Why it matters: A reviewer could argue the observed curve is mainly a *decision rule* phenomenon: with high false negatives, majority-like thresholds punish larger K, and M affects K mechanically. To firmly support the structural claim, you need to show that, holding the decision rule fixed (or optimally tuned), performance decreases with more sequential cycles.

Actionable fix:
- Add a factorial experiment:
  - Fix decision rule (e.g., single-rollout, any-positive, calibrated-prob threshold) and vary M.
  - Separately, fix M and vary K to isolate parallelism.
  - For consensus, tune $\tau$ per K on a dev set (or report a curve over $\tau$) to avoid unfair strictness artifacts.
- Report mean±95% CI for each M in the table and include #episodes.

Mentor Revised Version:
To isolate the structural effect of sequential depth, we (i) fix a decision rule (e.g., single-rollout acceptance or a calibrated-probability threshold) and vary $M$ while keeping $B$ fixed, and (ii) separately vary $K$ at fixed $M$ to quantify the marginal value of parallel rollouts. For consensus, we report performance as a function of $\tau$ for each $K$ to avoid threshold-induced artifacts. We include 95% bootstrap CIs for each point in Fig. 2.

References:
[4] Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents 2506.12928
annotations.summary: Cycle-reduction analysis is suggestive but confounded by varying τ/aggregation with K; add a cleaner factorial design (M × decision rule × τ) and report confidence intervals in the M-sweep figure/table.

annotations.text:
To understand why sequential verification fails, we analyze episodes where chunked verification (B) succeeded but sequential (A) failed. Table 2 shows the breakdown of 81 such episodes.
Trajectory drift accounts for 60.5% of cases where chunked verification outperforms sequential. In these episodes, the sequential verifier rejected a checkout (often a false negative), causing the agent to re-browse. During re-browsing, the agent frequently selected a worse product than the one originally found. Chunked verification avoids this by spending the entire budget upfront: if the first verification cycle fails, the agent gets a second chance without the re-browsing step that leads to trajectory drift. Only 2 episodes showed the reverse pattern (A succeeded, B failed), yielding a net benefit of 79 additional successes from chunked verification.
annotations.comment:
Page 5 - Experiments (4.4 Failure Analysis)

Problem: The failure analysis is informative but statistically biased because it conditions on episodes where **B succeeded and A failed**. This selection can inflate the apparent share of “trajectory drift” among those specific episodes, and it does not quantify how often drift occurs overall. Also, the text sometimes uses “chunked verification” to refer to (B), but the best-performing method is (C); it is unclear whether the drift analysis should be done for (C vs A) instead. Finally, “trajectory drift” is described qualitatively; readers need an operational definition (e.g., did the agent previously view a product that would satisfy constraints but later checked out a worse product after a rejection?).

Why it matters: “Trajectory drift is dominant” is a central mechanistic claim. If it is based on a conditioned subset and not robust across comparisons (A vs C), reviewers may discount the mechanism as post-hoc.

Actionable fix:
- Add symmetric analyses:
  (i) episodes where A succeeds but B fails (and characterize why);
  (ii) episodes where C succeeds but A fails (since C is your strongest method);
  (iii) unconditional frequency of each failure pattern across all episodes.
- Provide an explicit labeling rubric for failure categories and inter-annotator agreement if labeling is manual.

Mentor Revised Version:
To avoid selection bias, we report failure-pattern frequencies both (a) unconditionally over all episodes and (b) conditionally for each pairwise set (B succeeds/A fails, A succeeds/B fails, and C succeeds/A fails). We define trajectory drift operationally as cases where the agent had previously reached a product page that would later be judged successful, but after a verifier rejection it re-browsed and eventually checked out a different product that fails the evaluator constraints.

References:
[8] AgentRewardBench: Evaluating Automatic Evaluations of Web Agent Trajectories 2504.08942
annotations.summary: Failure analysis conditions on ‘B succeeds, A fails’ which biases mechanism attribution; need symmetric analysis (A succeeds, B fails), matched comparison to C, and a clearer operational definition of ‘trajectory drift’.

annotations.text:
One might hypothesize that chunked verification benefits from stochastic diversity across parallel rollouts. To test this, we compare performance under stochastic (temperature 0.7) and deterministic (temperature 0.0) world model decoding. Table 3 shows the results using $M = 2 , K = 5 , \tau = 0 . 5$ configuration.
The chunked verification advantage persists under deterministic decoding—in fact, it slightly increases from +7.67 pp to +9.67 pp. Under temperature 0, all K rollouts produce identical predictions (pˆ is always 0 or 1), eliminating any benefit from stochastic diversity. This confirms that the advantage comes from the structural benefit of reduced sequential cycles, not from aggregating diverse predictions.
annotations.comment:
Page 5 - Experiments (4.5 Temperature Ablation)

Problem: The temperature ablation is a good idea, but it is run under a configuration ($M=2,K=5,\tau=0.5$) that differs from the headline configuration ($M=1,K=10$ with $\tau=0.1$ in Condition B and single-rollout in C). This makes it hard to conclude that the *main* improvement is structural, because the temperature ablation does not directly test the main setting.

Why it matters: You want to claim that the improvement comes from reduced sequential cycles, not from stochastic diversity across rollouts. To make this claim robust, the ablation should be performed under the same $M,K$ settings that produce the headline gains.

Actionable fix:
- Add temperature=0 vs 0.7 comparisons for both $M=1,K=10$ and $M=10,K=1$.
- If the world model is deterministic at temp=0, clarify whether the actor is still stochastic; actor stochasticity could still induce drift.

Mentor Revised Version:
We repeat the temperature ablation under the main configurations ($M=1,K=10$ and $M=10,K=1$) to directly test whether the headline gains depend on stochastic diversity. Under temperature 0, the verifier produces identical rollouts for a fixed state; if chunked verification still outperforms the sequential baseline, this supports the claim that the benefit is driven by reduced sequential re-planning rather than sample diversity.

References:
[4] Scaling Test-time Compute for LLM Agents 2506.12928
annotations.summary: Temperature ablation supports ‘not stochastic diversity’, but it mixes settings (M=2,K=5,τ=0.5) and doesn’t test M=1; add a targeted ablation to isolate structural effect under the exact main configuration.

annotations.text:
The world model is poorly calibrated as a confidence estimator. Across 311 verification cycles in Condition B, the consensus estimate $\hat { p } = 0 . 0$ for 98.4% of cycles (306/311), with Brier score 0.28 and expected calibration error (ECE) 0.28. When $\hat { p } = 0 . 0$ , the actual success rate is 27.5% (84/306 successes)—far from the predicted 0%. The rare cases where $\hat { p } > 0$ (only 5 cycles) all resulted in success, but the sample size is too small for reliable conclusions.
This extreme concentration of predictions at $\hat { p } = 0 . 0$ explains why consensus aggregation does not help: when all K rollouts predict failure, majority voting cannot recover the correct answer. The benefit of chunked verification comes entirely from the structural change (fewer sequential cycles), not from the aggregation rule. For practitioners, this suggests that when using poorly-calibrated world models, the priority should be minimizing sequential verification cycles rather than investing in sophisticated aggregation schemes.
annotations.comment:
Page 6 - Experiments (4.6 Why Consensus Aggregation Fails)

Problem: The calibration statistics are a strong part of the paper, but the reporting is not yet sufficient to fully trust/interpret them:
- It is unclear whether Brier/ECE are computed at the *cycle* level (311 cycles) or *episode* level (600 episodes), and what the ground-truth label is in each case.
- ECE depends on binning; bin count/strategy is not stated.
- Given the extreme mass at $\hat p=0$, a reliability diagram (or cumulative calibration plot) is essential to show where miscalibration occurs.
- The conclusion “benefit comes entirely from structural change” is too strong given the observed decision-rule differences (single-rollout vs consensus) and the threshold interaction discussed earlier.

Why it matters: Your main contribution C3 is about “consensus degenerates due to calibration.” If the calibration computation is unclear, or if ECE is unstable under extreme class imbalance, reviewers may discount the calibration argument. Also, the practical guidance depends on whether calibration can be improved (e.g., via confidence elicitation or recalibration).

Actionable fix:
- Specify precisely: dataset (cycles), label definition, binning scheme, and whether $\hat p$ is a probability estimate or a Monte Carlo frequency.
- Add a reliability diagram + a table stratified by $\hat p$ bucket.
- Consider adding a simple recalibration baseline (temperature scaling / isotonic / verbalized confidence) or at least discuss why it is hard here.

Mentor Revised Version:
We evaluate verifier calibration at the verification-cycle level by treating each cycle’s $\hat p$ as a Monte Carlo estimate of success probability and using the realized checkout outcome as ground truth. We report Brier score, ECE (with a stated binning scheme), and a reliability diagram to visualize miscalibration under the highly skewed prediction distribution. While severe under-confidence explains why majority-style consensus rarely passes, we interpret the overall performance gap as arising from both (i) sequential re-planning effects and (ii) brittleness of strict aggregation under miscalibration.

References:
[6] When Can We Trust LLM Graders? Calibrating Confidence for Automated Assessment 2603.29559

[7] A Survey of Confidence Estimation and Calibration in Large Language Models 2311.08298
annotations.summary: Calibration diagnosis is valuable, but needs fuller reporting (reliability diagram, bins, class balance) and a check that Brier/ECE are computed on comparable units (cycle vs episode). Also temper ‘entirely structural’ claim.

annotations.text:
We studied how to allocate a fixed verification budget when using world models to verify irreversible actions. Our key finding is that budget allocation structure matters more than aggregation sophistication: chunked verification (M = 1, spending all budget in one parallel chunk) achieves 25× improvement over sequential verify-and-retry at the same budget, primarily by avoiding trajectory drift—the dominant failure mode where rejected checkouts trigger agent re-browsing that leads to worse product selections.
Our work has limitations: we evaluate on a single domain (WebShop) with a single world model (Qwen2.5-7B), and absolute success rates remain modest (21.50%). Future work should investigate whether these findings generalize to other domains with irreversible actions, explore bettercalibrated world models that could benefit from consensus aggregation, and develop adaptive budget allocation strategies that adjust M based on task difficulty.
annotations.comment:
Page 6 - Conclusion

Problem: The conclusion repeats strong statements (“budget allocation structure matters more…”, “trajectory drift—the dominant failure mode”) without fully qualifying the boundary conditions established by the experiments: single environment, single verifier, and decision-rule confounds. It also does not translate findings into a minimal actionable recipe that is robust under miscalibration (e.g., choose M small; avoid strict consensus; use calibrated threshold or permissive aggregator).

Why it matters: Conclusions are often where reviewers look for overclaiming. Tightening scope and giving a clear, defensible practitioner rule increases acceptance odds.

Actionable fix:
- Add 1–2 sentences listing boundary conditions explicitly (irreversible commit; verifier under-confidence; agent re-planning changes candidate set).
- Add a concrete “minimal recommendation” and an “if calibrated then…” alternative.
- Add a short generalization plan: evaluate on another domain with irreversible actions (e.g., WebArena flows) and with at least one better-calibrated verifier.

Mentor Revised Version:
We find that, for verifier-gated irreversible actions in WebShop, allocating a fixed verification budget into fewer sequential cycles can substantially improve success by reducing rejection-induced re-planning that drifts the browsing trajectory. This effect is most pronounced when the verifier is severely under-confident, in which case strict consensus rules rarely pass and can be counterproductive. Practically, when using a poorly calibrated verifier, a simple and robust default is to minimize the number of sequential verify-and-retry cycles (small $M$) and avoid overly strict aggregation; when calibration improves, more principled thresholding or aggregation may become beneficial. Future work should validate these conclusions across additional irreversible-action domains and across verifiers with different calibration profiles.

References:
[9] ARTIS: Agentic Risk-Aware Test-Time Scaling via Iterative Simulation 2602.01709
annotations.summary: Conclusion appropriately notes limitations but still overstates ‘dominant failure mode’ and ‘M=1 guidance’; add clearer boundary conditions, a minimal decision rule, and a concrete generalization plan across tasks/models.
